ddx.step1_summary:
- Chief complaint: Painful urination (dysuria) for a few days.
- Symptoms: Stinging/burning on passing urine for ~3 days; lower abdominal (suprapubic) crampy pain; small amount of visible blood in urine earlier today; urine smells "a bit weird"; no increased urinary frequency reported; no vaginal discharge noted; no fever, no flank/back pain, no nausea/vomiting.
- Onset/duration/severity/aggravating-alleviating: Started a few days ago, intermittent stinging with voiding, bothersome but not unbearable; tried OTC bicarbonate with no benefit; advised fluids and antibiotics by clinician.
- Past medical history: Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS). No other chronic medical problems reported.
- Medications/allergies: No regular medications. Allergic to clindamycin (swelling). Recently tried over-the-counter bicarbonate.
- Family/social history: No known family history of kidney/bladder disease. Lives with flatmates, 19-year-old female college student. Non-smoker, social alcohol. Sexually active with a single boyfriend for a couple months; uses condoms. Reports never having had an STD screen.
- Vital signs/exam findings: No formal vitals or physical exam recorded in the transcript; clinician noted no fever reported by patient and no flank pain on history.
- Labs/imaging: None documented (no urine dipstick, microscopy, culture, pregnancy test, or imaging performed in transcript).

V: Urolithiasis (ureteric or bladder stone): Hematuria and suprapubic/colicky pain can be caused by stones; young adults can present with lower urinary tract stone symptoms even without flank radiation.
I: Acute uncomplicated cystitis (bladder infection/UTI): Classic dysuria, suprapubic cramping, malodorous urine and hematuria are typical; common in young sexually active females.
Urethritis due to STI (Chlamydia trachomatis or Neisseria gonorrhoeae): Dysuria with little or no vaginal discharge, sexually active, never screened for STIs — can present similarly to UTI.

Acute pyelonephritis: Infectious involvement of upper tract can follow untreated lower UTI; would expect fever, flank pain, systemic symptoms (absent here) but still a consideration if symptoms worsen.
N: Bladder neoplasm (urothelial carcinoma): Can cause painless hematuria; extremely unlikely at age 19 but included for completeness.
D: Interstitial cystitis / painful bladder syndrome: Chronic bladder pain and dysuria without infection; usually longer history and more chronic symptoms, but can present with dysuria and suprapubic discomfort.
I2: Chemical/irritant cystitis (eg, exposure to spermicides, hygiene products, or recent medications): Can cause dysuria and urinary irritation; consider if topical irritants or recent exposures.
Medication-induced urinary symptoms: certain drugs (e.g., cyclophosphamide) cause hemorrhagic cystitis — unlikely here given medication history.
C: Congenital urinary tract abnormality (eg, vesicoureteral reflux, anatomic anomaly): Predisposes to recurrent UTIs, but less likely as first presentation in a 19-year-old without recurrent history.
A: Allergic/contact dermatitis of vulva (eg, latex allergy to condoms): Could cause local irritation and dysuria if there is vulvar inflammation; patient reports condom use but no itching/rash noted.
T: Urethral trauma from sexual activity: Recent sexual activity could cause urethral irritation, minor bleeding and dysuria if there was mechanical trauma.
E: Diabetes mellitus increasing UTI risk: Hyperglycemia predisposes to recurrent/complicated infections; no symptoms/signs reported to suggest diabetes, but metabolic risk increases infection risk.

step3_ranked_ddx.diagnosis: Acute uncomplicated cystitis (lower urinary tract infection)
step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Young sexually active female with several days of dysuria, suprapubic cramping, malodorous urine and an episode of visible hematuria — classic features for acute cystitis. Clinician also concluded this was most likely and planned empirical antibiotics.
supporting_evidence: Burning/stinging pain on urination for a few days
Visible blood in urine earlier today
Sexually active female (risk factor), no recent STD screen
opposing_evidence: No increased urinary frequency or urgency reported (commonly present but not required)
No urine dipstick/micro results documented to confirm pyuria/bacteriuria
No fever or systemic symptoms (but consistent with uncomplicated lower UTI)

step3_ranked_ddx.diagnosis: Urethritis due to sexually transmitted infection (Chlamydia or Gonorrhea)
step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Sexually active patient who has never had STI screening presents with dysuria and minimal vaginal symptoms — urethritis from chlamydia or gonorrhea can present with dysuria and may lack obvious discharge. Important alternative because management differs (need NAAT testing and partner notification).
supporting_evidence: Dysuria without prominent frequency/urgency (can be urethritis)
No vaginal discharge reported (urethral infection may present without obvious vaginal symptoms)
Sexually active, no prior STI screening
opposing_evidence: Presence of suprapubic crampy pain and malodorous urine + hematuria more suggestive of bladder infection
No history of unprotected sex (uses condoms) and single partner for months (though condoms not 100% protective and use details uncertain)
No penile/partner symptoms documented but absence does not exclude STI

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Hematuria and lower abdominal pain can be caused by a stone in the lower urinary tract or bladder; dysuria can occur if stone irritates urethra/bladder. Less likely given lack of severe colicky flank pain or radiation to groin/back and relative mild systemic signs.
supporting_evidence: Lower abdominal pain and dysuria could be due to a lower tract stone
opposing_evidence: No flank pain or severe colicky pain typical of ureteric stones
No history of prior stones or risk factors discussed
Malodorous urine and burning on urination more typical of infection

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Possible progression from lower UTI upward, but currently unlikely because patient denies fever, flank/back pain, or systemic illness. Important to consider if symptoms worsen or fever/back pain develop.
supporting_evidence: Hematuria can be present with upper tract infection
History of dysuria and bladder symptoms could ascend if untreated
opposing_evidence: No fever, chills, or flank pain reported

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Chronic bladder pain conditions can present with dysuria and suprapubic pain, but typically are chronic and associated with urinary frequency/urgency and longer symptom duration — less likely with an acute few-day onset and hematuria.
supporting_evidence: Absence of fever or systemic infection signs
opposing_evidence: Acute onset over a few days rather than chronic course
Hematuria and malodorous urine more suggest infection
Young age and first episode make primary interstitial cystitis less likely
